text.tspan: The one place where words talk to each other

Everything before this page treated each word on its own: its id, its embedding, its position. Attention is the first — and the only — place where one word can collect information from the others. Picture every word asking a question ("who in this sentence matters to me?") while every word also holds up a label
that might answer it. In the code the question is
(the key), and what a word hands over when it is chosen is
(the value). These four lines compare every question with every label, turn those comparisons into shares that add up to
, and rebuild each word as a blend of the words it
found most relevant. A whole Transformer is a stack of exactly this, with some per-word arithmetic in between.

text.tspan: Now every query meets every key. Cell
is the dot product of query row i with key row j: multiply the two rows
multiplications — and add the results. A large positive total means "these two point the same
way", a negative one means "these point apart". For example, in sequence A the word "the"
against "sat". Section B works one of these sums out by hand. Notice how big the numbers
terms produces large totals, and that is exactly what the next line fixes.

text.tspan: turns score GAPS into shares, and it
exaggerates big gaps enormously. With raw totals this large, one key would grab almost the whole share and the model
would have nothing left to learn from — a nearly all-or-nothing
passes back almost no gradient during training.

Softmax, opened up into the steps a calculator would do

Softmax is usually treated as a black box. Opened up, it is three plain steps: subtract the row’s largest score (this changes nothing in the result, it only keeps the numbers small enough for the computer), raise e to every value, then divide by the total. Watch the

What the division by the square root of
Here is the same row softmaxed twice: once with the division by √
, once without. Without it, the biggest score swallows almost the whole row. That looks decisive, but it is bad for learning: when one key already has nearly
barely changes anything, so the gradient that training depends on nearly vanishes.
the same row, softmaxed two ways
Without the division, the top key takes
of this row and the weakest real key gets less than
. With it, the same row runs from
: every word still gets a real share. That matters because a
that is nearly all-or-nothing gives training almost no signal, so attention
would get stuck on whichever key happened to win first. And this is only
— the wider the heads, the bigger the effect, which is exactly why the divisor grows with √
instead of being a fixed number.
